turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no regard for misfortunes which involve nothing but what is dishonorable.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I cannot, Miss Bennet, permit myself to consider a person in connexion with any idea of impropriety or dishonour. No one can be faultless, and he is not the first of your acquaintance who has injured me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no idea what you mean, sir, but I am afraid, from the manner in which you express yourself, that you know nothing at all of the subject you are discussing.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I do not seek to justify myself before you, Miss Bennet, but I must assert that my understanding of Wickham's character is far more accurate than yours.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your understanding of Mr. Wickham might be more accurate, but your perception of people in general leaves much to be desired. You seem blind to your own faults.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your candor is commendable, but your criticism is unjust. I am aware of my shortcomings, but they do not negate the sincerity of my feelings.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your feelings are not at all a subject of my concern. Your proposal was an insult to my understanding, and your manner has injured me deeply.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am well aware of the pain my actions have caused you, Miss Bennet, but I cannot deny the truth of my feelings, however unpleasant it may be for both of us.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your feelings, sir, are entirely your own concern at present. You sought my hand with a paltry regard and I cannot think you deserve my sympathy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words wound me, but I understand your sentiments. I can only hope that time and reflection may alter your opinion of me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I am truly sorry if my words have caused you pain, but I cannot alter my opinion of your character based on your sudden and unexplained declaration of affection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I must be frank: the very last thing I expected to hear from you was a confession of love. Your past actions have given me reason to distrust you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I am aware of the depth of your displeasure towards me. I have, however, been compelled to lay my heart bare, though it may cost me your goodwill.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your words may indeed cost me goodwill, Mr. Darcy, for they reveal much about your character that I find difficult to overlook. Yet, I cannot deny the sincerity in your tone, though my heart remains unchanged.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your candor is both surprising and appreciated. I am not unaccustomed to being disliked, but your disapproval has been a source of profound discomfort to me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your declaration, though unexpected, does not alter my longstanding opinion of your actions and character. I must be honest: I find it difficult to reconcile your words of love with the pain you have caused others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your insight cuts deeply, yet I am here to make amends for my past errors. Your rejection would be just, but I cannot bear the thought of it without offering you a full account of my transformation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, while your intentions to amend may be sincere, I must confess that my feelings towards you are not easily swayed. Your past actions have left a deep impression.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your discernment is a formidable challenge, but I am resolved to earn your esteem, though I may fail. I offer my heart with humility, hoping for the chance to prove myself worthy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your sincerity is commendable, but my feelings towards you have been shaped by more than just your recent actions. I will not pretend to welcome your declaration.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
